standard_text: Given a numeric expression with common rational number bases and integer exponents, apply the properties of exponents to generate equivalent expressions.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to apply the properties of integer exponents, product of powers, quotient of powers, power of a power, power of a product, zero exponent, and negative exponents, to generate equivalent numerical expressions. The on-grade work builds from matching a power to its expanded notation, through each named rule one at a time, to combining several rules in one expression. Every rule rests on one idea: an exponent counts how many times the base is used as a factor. Students who stall here usually carry older gaps, most often weak multiplication fact and factor knowledge from grade 4 and a shaky grasp of exponent notation from grade 6. Intervention should rebuild those foundations, then the grade 7 skills of prime factorization with exponents and squares and square roots, before returning to the rules themselves.

steps.rationale: The Below-proficiency recognition gate the item spec names: match a power expression to its equivalent expanded notation using positive exponents. Seeing (5^2)^3 as three copies of 5^2 is the concrete proof the later rules abstract, and the first line of defense against adding exponents where they should multiply.

The first named property and the foundation of the others: product of powers, a^m x a^n = a^(m+n). This Approaching-proficiency move is where the standard's two great errors -- multiplying the bases and multiplying the exponents -- must be defeated before anything else builds.

The two mirror rules for a single common base: quotient of powers (subtract the exponents) and power of a power (multiply them). Placed after the product rule because both are contrasted against it, and students must learn to pick the right operation for the situation.

The two least intuitive named properties -- zero exponent (a^0 = 1) and negative exponent (a^(-n) = 1/a^n) -- taught as consequences of the subtraction rule. The spec's 1/27 and value-of-a-equals-0 items live here; hand-authored because no engine stem isolates this move.

The At-proficiency task: apply more than one property in one expression, resolving the power of a power before the product. This requires every single-property rule to already be automatic, so it sits after S1-S4.

The Above-proficiency reversal: given an equation with a missing exponent, run the property backward and verify by substitution. Only possible once each forward rule is fluent, so it is the capstone that bridges toward Algebra I exponent work.

skills.name: Find factor pairs and identify prime and composite numbers

prerequisite_skill.description: List all factor pairs of a whole number within 100 and tell whether a number is prime or composite.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: List all the factor pairs of 12. Is 7 prime or composite?

skills.i_do_script: A factor pair is two whole numbers that multiply to make my number. Watch 12: I can build it as an array 1 row of 12, 2 rows of 6, or 3 rows of 4, so the factor pairs are 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. I check the counting numbers in order, 1, 2, 3, 4, and stop when the pairs start repeating. A number like 7 has only one array, 1 row of 7, so its only factors are 1 and 7: that makes it prime. A number with more than two factors, like 12, is composite.

canonical_error.pattern: Misses factor pairs by not checking numbers in order, or calls any odd number prime
canonical_error.example: Says the factors of 12 are just 2, 6, and 12, or says 9 is prime because it is odd
canonical_error.why: The student guesses factors instead of testing 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, and confuses odd with prime. 9 = 3 x 3, so 9 has three factors and is composite.

skills.item_template: A whole number within 100. Student lists factor pairs, names a missing factor, or classifies the number as prime or composite. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: List all the factor pairs of 12.
List all the factor pairs of 18.
What number completes the factor pair? 4 x ___ = 36
Is 15 prime or composite?
Is 13 prime or composite?
List all the factors of 20.
Which numbers are prime: 2, 9, 11, 21?
What number completes the factor pair? 6 x ___ = 48

redirect_script.stop: Did you test the numbers in order, starting at 1?
redirect_script.prompt: Check 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. For each one that divides your number evenly, write the pair. Stop when the pairs start to repeat. Prime means exactly two factors, 1 and itself, not just odd.
redirect_script.praise: You tested factors in order and caught every pair, that is the whole method.

vocabulary.definition: Two whole numbers that multiply to make a given number, like 3 and 4 for 12.
A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, like 7.
A number with more than two factors, like 12.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 multiplication facts and arrays (build a number as equal rows of dots).

Can you build 12 as 4 rows? 5 rows? Which ones work?
Every array that works gives a factor pair: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. After 3 the pairs repeat, so we have them all.
If a student skips 3 and 4, ask 'did you test every number in order, or jump around?'
Your turn: build arrays for 18 and list its factor pairs. Then try 7. How many arrays does 7 have?

skills.name: Read exponent notation and evaluate a small power

prerequisite_skill.description: Expand a power into repeated multiplication and find its value.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Write 3^4 as a multiplication. What is 2^3?

skills.i_do_script: An exponent counts how many times the base is used as a factor. Watch 3^4: the base is 3 and the exponent is 4, so I write four 3s multiplied: 3 x 3 x 3 x 3. To find the value I multiply left to right: 3 x 3 = 9, 9 x 3 = 27, 27 x 3 = 81. The trap is reading 3^4 as 3 x 4 = 12. The exponent is a count of factors, not a number to multiply by. Compare on a doubling chain: 2^3 doubles 1 three times, 1, 2, 4, 8, and lands on 8, not on 2 x 3 = 6.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the base by the exponent instead of using the base as a repeated factor
canonical_error.example: Writes 3^4 = 3 x 4 = 12 instead of 3 x 3 x 3 x 3 = 81
canonical_error.why: The student treats the exponent like a second factor. The exponent is a count: 3^4 means four 3s multiplied together, so the value is 81, not 12.

skills.item_template: A power with a small whole-number base and exponent, value under about 1000. Student expands it or evaluates it. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Write 3^4 as repeated multiplication.
Write 2^5 as repeated multiplication.
What is 2^3?
What is 5^2?
What is 3^3?
What is 10^3?

What is 2^4?

redirect_script.stop: Is the exponent a count, or something you multiply by?
redirect_script.prompt: The exponent counts how many times the base is a factor. For 3^4, write the 3 four times, 3 x 3 x 3 x 3, then multiply left to right. It is not 3 x 4.
redirect_script.praise: You used the base as a factor the right number of times, that is what the exponent means.

vocabulary.definition: The number being multiplied repeatedly; in 3^4 the base is 3.
The small raised number that counts how many times the base is used as a factor; in 3^4 the exponent is 4.
An expression like 2^3 that means a base multiplied by itself a number of times.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 6 exponent notation with a doubling chain and expanded products.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a doubling chain on a number line: 1 to 2 to 4 to 8, one hop per doubling.
Three doublings land on 8. Is that the same as 2 x 3?
No. 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, but 2 x 3 = 6. The exponent 3 counts the factors, it is not something we multiply by.
If a student answers 6, point at the chain: 'where does the third doubling land?'
Your turn: expand 3^4 and find its value.

steps.annotation: The exponent counts how many times the base is a factor.

check.prompt: What does the exponent 2 tell you to do with the 4?
check.answer: use it as a factor twice

steps.annotation: Multiply, do not add.
Two factors of 4.

check.prompt: Who answers 8 for 4^2? What did they do instead?
check.answer: multiplied base by exponent — 4 x 2, but 4^2 is 4 x 4

steps.annotation: The exponent counts the factors.
Multiply the two copies.

Multiply the copies, a pair at a time.
Name the Trap — what do you get by multiplying base times exponent? Why is that wrong?

practice_problems.answer: The student treats the exponent like a second factor. The exponent is a count: 3^4 means four 3s multiplied together, so the value is 81, not 12.

skills.name: Write the prime factorization of a whole number using exponents

prerequisite_skill.description: Break a whole number (200 or less) into a product of primes and write repeated primes with exponents.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Write the prime factorization of 72 using exponents.

skills.i_do_script: Prime factorization breaks a number all the way down to prime factors, and exponents collect the repeats. Watch 72 on a factor tree: 72 = 8 x 9. Neither is prime, so keep splitting: 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 and 9 = 3 x 3. Now every branch ends in a prime: 2, 2, 2, 3, 3. I collect the repeats with exponents: three 2s is 2^3 and two 3s is 3^2, so 72 = 2^3 x 3^2. Check by multiplying back: 8 x 9 = 72. A prime number like 17 is already done; its prime factorization is just 17.

canonical_error.pattern: Stops at composite factors or writes the exponent as the number of different primes instead of the count of repeats
canonical_error.example: Writes 90 = 9 x 10 and stops, or pools the primes into 2 x 3^3 (= 54) instead of 2 x 3^2 x 5
canonical_error.why: The student either quits before every branch is prime or loses track of which prime repeats how many times. Each exponent counts the copies of one prime: three 2s and two 3s, so 2^3 x 3^2.

skills.item_template: A whole number 200 or less. Student writes its prime factorization using exponents, or identifies the number a given prime factorization builds. Numeric or expression response, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Write the prime factorization of 12 using exponents.
Write the prime factorization of 72 using exponents.
Write the prime factorization of 40 using exponents.
Write the prime factorization of 100 using exponents.
Which is the prime factorization of 36?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 36 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 2^2 x 3^2. 4 x 9 and 6^2 stop at composite factors; 2^3 x 3 is 24, a miscount of the 2s.

sample_items.stem: What number has the prime factorization 2 x 3^2 x 5?
Write the prime factorization of 17.
Write the prime factorization of 150 using exponents.

redirect_script.stop: Is every factor at the end of your tree prime?
redirect_script.prompt: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime. Then count the copies of each prime and write that count as its exponent: three 2s is 2^3. Check by multiplying everything back together.
redirect_script.praise: Every branch is prime and each exponent counts its repeats, that is a complete prime factorization.

vocabulary.definition: A number written as a product of only prime numbers, like 72 = 2^3 x 3^2.
A diagram that splits a number into factors again and again until every branch is prime.
The small raised number that counts how many copies of a factor appear; 2^3 means three 2s.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a factor tree for 72: split into 8 x 9, then 8 into 2 x 2 x 2 and 9 into 3 x 3. Circle each prime at the bottom.
Why do we keep splitting 8 and 9? How do we know when to stop?
We stop when every circled number is prime. Count the circles: three 2s and two 3s, so 72 = 2^3 x 3^2. The exponent counts the copies.
If a student writes 72 = 8 x 9 and stops, ask 'is 8 prime? is 9 prime?'
Your turn: draw a tree for 60 and write its prime factorization with exponents.

practice_problems.stem: Write the prime factorization of 6.
Write the prime factorization of 9 using an exponent.
Write the prime factorization of 24 using exponents.
Write the prime factorization of 45 using exponents.
Write the prime factorization of 120 using exponents.
What number has the prime factorization 2^2 x 3 x 5?
Two different factor trees for 48 are started: 48 = 6 x 8 and 48 = 4 x 12. Finish both. Do they give the same prime factorization?
practice_problems.answer: Yes, both give 2^4 x 3. The starting split does not change the primes at the bottom.

practice_problems.stem: Deja wrote the prime factorization of 54. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She stopped while 6 was still composite. Split 6 into 2 x 3, so 54 = 2 x 3 x 3^2 = 2 x 3^3. Check: 2 x 27 = 54.

activities.title: Tree to the Primes
activities.instructions:
1. Build 36 with tiles as a 6 by 6 square, then split it: 6 x 6.
2. Split each 6 into 2 x 3 on a factor tree and circle every prime.
3. Count the circles and write the exponent form: 2^2 x 3^2.
4. Repeat with 40 and 72, starting each tree two different ways to see the primes come out the same.
5. Say each time: split until every branch is prime, then count the copies.

activities.title: Number Meets Its Primes
materials: Card deck: number cards and prime factorization cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each number card (like 72) to its exponent-form prime factorization card (like 2^3 x 3^2).
3. To claim a match, multiply the factorization back out loud and land on the number.
4. Two decoy cards contain a composite factor or a wrong exponent; set them aside and explain the error.

strategy_links.why: Tiles and factor trees make 'split until prime, then count the copies' visible before the exponent shorthand is named.
Stopping at a composite factor is a stable, predictable error; finding and fixing it in shown work confronts it directly.
Thinking aloud 'is this branch prime yet?' models the self-check that keeps a tree going to completion.

questioning_prompts: Is every number at the bottom of your tree prime? How do you know?
How many copies of 2 are in your tree? What exponent records that?
If you start the tree with a different split, will the primes change?
How can you check your factorization is right?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops the tree at composite factors like 8 x 9.
misconception_redirects.say: Is 8 prime? Is 9? Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime you can circle.
misconception_redirects.praise: You split all the way down, now every factor is prime.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the wrong exponent, like 2^2 x 3 for 24.

misconception_redirects.praise: You matched each exponent to its count of copies and verified by multiplying back.

skills.name: Evaluate squares and find square roots of perfect squares

prerequisite_skill.description: Square a whole number and find the square root of a perfect square up to 400, using the inverse relationship.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 7^2? What is the square root of 144?

skills.i_do_script: Squaring and square roots undo each other, and a square array shows why. Watch 7^2: a 7 by 7 square of tiles holds 7 x 7 = 49 tiles, so 7^2 = 49. The square root asks the reverse question: 49 tiles make a square with how many on each side? Seven, so the square root of 49 is 7. The trap is doubling: 7^2 is not 7 x 2 = 14, and the square root of 100 is not 50. Squaring multiplies a number by itself; the root finds the side of the square.

canonical_error.pattern: Doubles instead of squaring, or halves instead of taking the square root
canonical_error.example: Says 7^2 = 14, or says the square root of 100 is 50
canonical_error.why: The student swaps 'times itself' for 'times 2'. A square has equal sides: 7^2 = 7 x 7 = 49, and the square root of 100 is 10 because 10 x 10 = 100, not 100 divided by 2.

skills.item_template: A whole number to square, or a perfect square up to 400 to take the square root of. Numeric response or multiple choice, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: What is 6^2?
What is 9^2?
What is the square root of 64?
What is the square root of 144?
What is the square root of 100?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 10 x 10 = 100. 50 halves instead of rooting; 25 is 100 divided by 4; 1000 multiplies by 10.

sample_items.stem: What is 13^2?

sample_items.distractor_logic: 16 = 4^2 and 36 = 6^2. 20 and 50 sit between squares (16 and 25, 49 and 64), so no whole number multiplies by itself to make them.

redirect_script.stop: Did you multiply the number by itself, or by 2?
redirect_script.prompt: Squaring means times itself: 7^2 = 7 x 7 = 49. The square root asks 'what number times itself makes this?' For 100 that is 10, because 10 x 10 = 100. Picture the square: the root is the side length.
redirect_script.praise: You used the number times itself and its root as the side of the square, that is the inverse pair.

vocabulary.definition: A number that is a whole number times itself, like 49 = 7 x 7.
The number that multiplies by itself to make a given number; the square root of 49 is 7.
Two operations that undo each other, like squaring and taking the square root.

worked_example_script.text: Build a 7 by 7 square of tiles (or draw it on grid paper) and count by rows: 7, 14, 21, ... 49.
How many tiles are in the square? So what is 7^2?
49 tiles, so 7^2 = 49. Now reverse it: if a square holds 49 tiles, each side has 7. The square root of 49 is 7.
If a student says 7^2 = 14, point at the square: 'is this 7 doubled, or 7 rows of 7?'
Your turn: sketch the square for 9^2, then tell me the square root of 81.

activities.title: Build the Square, Find the Side
activities.instructions:
1. Partner A picks a side length from 3 to 10 and builds the square with tiles.
2. Partner B counts the tiles and writes the squaring equation, like 6^2 = 36.
3. Reverse: Partner A grabs a perfect-square pile of tiles (16, 25, 36, 49) and Partner B arranges them into a square to find the side, writing 'the square root of 36 is 6.'
4. Try to build a square from 20 tiles. It cannot be done, so 20 is not a perfect square.
5. Say each time: the square root is the side of the square.

activities.title: Square and Root Pairs
materials: Card deck: squaring cards, root cards, and value cards
activities.instructions:

2. Match each expression card (like 9^2 or 'square root of 169') to its value card.
3. To claim a match, say the multiplication that proves it, like 13 x 13 = 169.
4. Two decoy value cards come from doubling or halving; set them aside and explain the error.

strategy_links.why: Building actual squares from tiles makes 'root equals side length' concrete before the inverse rule is named.
Doubling and halving in place of squaring and rooting are precise errors a find-and-fix corrects head-on.
Choral response drills on the perfect squares to 15^2 build the recall that grade 8 exponent work leans on.

skills.name: Match a power expression to its equivalent expanded notation
skills.i_do_script: A power of a power tells me to use the WHOLE inner power as a factor. Watch (5^2)^3: the outer exponent 3 says use 5^2 three times: (5^2) x (5^2) x (5^2). Since each 5^2 is two 5s, that is six 5s in all, so (5^2)^3 = 5^6. The exponents multiply: 2 x 3 = 6. The trap is adding them (2 + 3 = 5) or losing count of how many copies to write.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the exponents (or writes the wrong number of copies) when expanding a power of a power instead of multiplying them
canonical_error.example: Expands (5^2)^3 as 5^2 x 5^3 = 5^5, adding 2 and 3 instead of writing three copies of 5^2 to get 5^6
canonical_error.why: The student confuses power of a power with product of powers. The outer exponent counts COPIES of the inner power, so the exponents multiply: (5^2)^3 = 5^(2 x 3) = 5^6, not 5^5.

skills.item_template: A power of a power with positive exponents. Student selects the equivalent expanded notation. Multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: An expression is given: (5^2)^3. Select the equivalent expanded notation.
sample_items.distractor_logic: (5^2)^3 = three copies of 5^2 = 5^6. Adding exponents gives the wrong 5^5; too few or too many copies give 5^4 or 5^8.

sample_items.stem: An expression is given: (3^2)^4. Select the equivalent expanded notation.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Four copies of 3^2 = 3^8. The distractors add exponents or write three copies instead of four.

sample_items.stem: Which expanded notation equals (2^3)^2?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Two copies of 2^3 = 2^6. Adding exponents gives 2^5; wrong copy counts give 2^4 or 2^9.

sample_items.stem: Write (5^2)^7 as a product of copies of 5^2, then as a single power.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The outer 7 means seven copies of 5^2, so 5^(2 x 7) = 5^14.

redirect_script.stop: Do the exponents add here, or multiply?
redirect_script.prompt: The outer exponent counts COPIES of the inner power. (5^2)^3 is three copies of 5^2, so write 5^2 three times: that is 5^6, because 2 x 3 = 6. It is not 5^2 x 5^3.
redirect_script.praise: You wrote the right number of copies and multiplied the exponents -- that's power of a power.

vocabulary.definition: A power raised to another exponent, like (5^2)^3; the exponents multiply.
An expression written out as a product of repeated factors, like (5^2) x (5^2) x (5^2).

skills.name: Find a missing exponent in an equation using the properties of exponents
skills.i_do_script: Before any rule, count factors: 2^7 is seven 2s multiplied together, and the 2^3 already hands me three of them -- so the mystery power has to supply exactly the rest. When an exponent is missing, I use the property in reverse and then check. Watch 2^a x 2^3 = 2^7: the product rule says a + 3 = 7, so a = 4. I check by substituting: 2^4 x 2^3 = 2^7 -- correct. For a quotient 5^a / 5^2 = 5^4, the rule says a - 2 = 4, so a = 6. The key is to write the exponent equation the property gives you, solve it, and always substitute back to confirm.

canonical_error.pattern: Sets up the wrong exponent operation, or guesses the missing exponent without checking it against the equation
canonical_error.example: For 5^a / 5^2 = 5^4 answers a = 2 (subtracting 4 - 2) instead of a = 6 (since a - 2 = 4 means a = 4 + 2)
canonical_error.why: The student mixes up which way the operation runs. A quotient means a - 2 = 4, so a = 6; a product means a + 3 = 7, so a = 4. Writing the property's exponent equation and substituting back catches the error.

skills.name: Simplify using the quotient of powers or power of a power rule
skills.i_do_script: Two more rules, both about like bases. Dividing like bases SUBTRACTS the exponents: 5^6 / 5^2 = 5^(6-2) = 5^4, because two of the six 5s on top cancel with the two on the bottom. Keep the base and pick the right operation for the exponents.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the wrong exponent operation -- adds a power of a power, or divides/adds the exponents in a quotient instead of subtracting

canonical_error.why: The student grabs the wrong rule. Quotient of powers SUBTRACTS the exponents (5^6 / 5^2 = 5^4); power of a power MULTIPLIES them ((3^2)^3 = 3^6). Neither adds, and neither divides the exponents.

skills.name: Rewrite expressions using zero and negative exponents
skills.i_do_script: Zero and negative exponents both come from the subtraction rule. Since 5^3 / 5^3 = 5^0 and any number over itself is 1, a^0 = 1 for any nonzero base -- so 7^0 = 1. skills.name: Apply more than one property of exponents to simplify an expression
skills.i_do_script: Why does a power of a power MULTIPLY the exponents? Expand it and count: (4^3)^2 means 4^3 times 4^3 -- write them out and you're looking at six factors of 4, so (4^3)^2 = 4^6. The rule 'multiply 3 x 2' is just counting those factors without writing them. Now a two-rule expression runs on counts all the way down: (4^3)^2 x 4^2 becomes 4^6 x 4^2 -- six 4s times two more 4s is eight 4s -- 4^8. I handle the power of a power first because until it's expanded into a single count, there's nothing for the product rule to add. When in doubt at ANY step, expand a small piece and count the factors -- the expansion is the proof.

canonical_error.why: The student skips the order of the properties. The power of a power must be resolved first (multiply the inner exponents), and only then do you add for the product. Adding everything ignores the parentheses.

skills.name: Solve for more than one missing exponent and critique a worked simplification
skills.i_do_script: Every missing exponent you have found so far had one answer. Watch what happens when two are missing: 6^a times 6^b over 6^3 equals 1 over 6^4. Same base, so I combine -- a plus b minus 3 on the left, and negative 4 on the right. That gives a + b - 3 = -4, so a + b = -1. I cannot pin down a, and I cannot pin down b, but I know exactly what they sum to. There are infinitely many answers and every one of them satisfies a + b = -1.

Students slide integer values into the two blanks until the totals match, then find a second pair that also matches -- the point lands when a second and third arrangement work equally well.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 6^a x 6^b / 6^3 = 1/6^4. Leave plenty of space underneath.
Same base everywhere. On the left, what happens to the exponents when I multiply, and then when I divide?
So the left side is 6 to the what? Say the expression using a and b.
Now the right side: 1 over 6^4. How do I write that as 6 to a single power?
If the student stalls and says there is not enough information, do not supply the answer. Ask them to write down the equation they DO have, then ask what it tells them about a and b together.
We have a + b - 3 = -4, so a + b = -1. Give me one pair that works. Now give me a completely different pair.
Both pairs check out. So what is the actual answer to this problem -- a pair of numbers, or something else?
The relationship is the answer. Some exponent equations pin down a value; this one pins down a sum, and every pair that fits is correct.

printable_artifact.title: When There Is More Than One Answer
printable_artifact.instructions: Combine to one exponent statement per side, then read what it determines.
items: Multiply, same base  ->  add exponents.   Divide  ->  subtract.   Power of a power  ->  multiply.
One unknown  ->  one answer.   Two unknowns in one equation  ->  a relationship.
Checking a critique: verify EVERY step, not just the last line.

practice_problems.stem: Write 1/3^5 as a power of 3 with a single exponent.
5^m x 5^n = 5^0. What must m + n equal?
6^a x 6^b / 6^3 = 1/6^4. Give one possible set of values for a and b.
practice_problems.answer: Any pair with a + b = -1, e.g. a = 0 and b = -1, or a = 2 and b = -3.
practice_problems.notes: The spec's own above-proficiency item. Ask for a second pair after the first -- that is where the idea lands.

practice_problems.stem: Select the three expressions equivalent to (4^3)^2 x 4^2, from: 4^8, 4^7, 4^6 x 4^2, 4^5 x 4^2, 1/4^8, 4^16/4^8.
practice_problems.notes: Three correct answers rather than one. 4^7 is the add-instead-of-multiply slip.

practice_problems.stem: 2^x x 2^y = 2^-6, and x is positive. Give a possible pair for x and y, and explain why y must be negative.
practice_problems.answer: x + y = -6, so with x positive, e.g. x = 2 and y = -8. y must be negative because a positive x already exceeds -6, so y has to pull the sum down past zero.
practice_problems.notes: Adds a constraint that narrows the family without collapsing it to one answer.

practice_problems.stem: Josie simplified an expression incorrectly. Find her error and simplify correctly.
practice_problems.answer: Step 3 is the error. Raising 2^2 to the power 2 multiplies the exponents: 2 x 2 = 4, so (2^2)^2 = 2^4. Josie carried the negative sign down from the original -3 exponent even though it had already been used in step 1. The correct simplification is 2^4, which is 16.
practice_problems.notes: Steps 1, 2, and 4 are all internally valid, so a student checking only the final line accepts it. The error is one step deep.

practice_problems.stem: 3^a / 3^b = 1. What does this tell you about a and b? How many pairs satisfy it?
practice_problems.answer: 3^(a-b) = 3^0, so a - b = 0, meaning a = b. Infinitely many pairs work, but they are constrained to be equal -- unlike a + b = -1, this relationship forces the two unknowns to match.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own exponent equation with two missing exponents whose answer is the relationship m + n = 4. Then write a second equation whose answer is m - n = 4. Trade with a partner.
practice_problems.answer: Any valid pair, e.g. 7^m x 7^n = 7^4 for the first, and 7^m / 7^n = 7^4 for the second. The multiplication or division decides which relationship falls out.
practice_problems.notes: Constructing the problem exposes whether the student knows which operation produces which relationship.

activities.title: Two Blanks, Many Fills
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out an equation frame with two blank exponent slots over a shared base and a target on the right.
2. Pairs fill both blanks with integer tiles so the equation holds, then record the pair.
3. Rule: a pair only scores if the team can find a SECOND different fill for the same frame.
4. After three frames, ask what all the winning fills for a frame had in common -- the relationship is what survives.
5. Close with a frame whose relationship is a - b = 0 and ask why the fills behave differently there.

activities.title: Josie's Third Step
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs verify each of Josie's four steps independently and mark each one right or wrong before discussing.
2. Ask first: how many steps are actually correct? (Three of four.)
3. Pairs name the property Josie misapplied in step 3 and state what it should have produced.
4. Pairs write the correct simplification and evaluate it as a whole number.
5. Debrief: what checking habit would have caught this, given that the final line looks perfectly reasonable?

content.error_step: Step 3 -- Josie raised 2^2 to the power 2 and produced 2^-4, reusing a negative sign that had already been consumed in step 1.
content.why: Power of a power multiplies exponents: 2 x 2 = 4, so (2^2)^2 = 2^4 = 16. Nothing in step 3 is negative; the -3 was used up when it combined with 5.

activities.title: Name the Relationship
activities.instructions:
1. Post an equation with two unknown exponents: 9^a x 9^b = 9^7, 5^a / 5^b = 5^-2, 4^a x 4^b = 1.
2. Students write the RELATIONSHIP, not a pair of values.
3. A correct relationship with no values scores full; a valid pair with no relationship scores half.
4. Final round: post one with a single unknown mixed in, so students have to notice which kind of answer the question wants.

strategy_links.why: Josie's four-step work sits beside a correct simplification, and only one step differs -- the contrast is the lesson.
Locating an error one step deep in otherwise valid work is exactly the above-proficiency demand in this standard.
Passing the whiteboard between partners for each exponent step surfaces the moment where add, subtract, and multiply get confused.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student assumes the two unknown exponents are equal to force one answer.

misconception_redirects.praise: Good -- you tested the assumption instead of keeping it because it made the problem familiar.

misconception_redirects.say: The last line can look right and still come from a broken step. Verify each step against the one above it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the steps, not the appearance of the answer.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5, applying more than one property in a single expression, the At-proficiency core. If they pass, move up to S6, finding a missing exponent. If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks prime factorization with exponents and B2 checks squares and square roots, the two grade 7 skills (7.NS.5 and 7.NS.6) the item spec names as looking back. pld_descriptors.note: Verbatim from the ILEARN item specification. These are performance bands on THIS standard, not lower-grade content: a student at Below Proficiency is working on this standard at its least complex entry point.
pld_descriptors.below: Apply the product of powers, power of a power, and negative exponent properties to identify equivalent, fully simplified numerical expressions using integer bases and exponents. Identify unknown exponents in simple equality statements involving a single exponent property.
pld_descriptors.approaching: Apply the product of powers, power of a power, negative exponent, and quotient of powers properties to generate or identify equivalent expressions, including expressions that are not fully simplified. Determine missing exponents in simple equality statements involving two properties.
pld_descriptors.at: Apply the product of powers, power of a power, negative exponent, quotient of powers, and zero exponent properties to generate or identify equivalent expressions, including those with fractional bases. Find missing exponents in complex expressions. Simplify expressions involving negative integers in the quotient property.
pld_descriptors.above: Apply multiple exponent properties flexibly to analyze, compare, and generate more than two equivalent expressions. Find the value of more than one missing exponent.
